title: Manual de Processos - Design (Process 3)
one_line_summary: A Portuguese-language internal design system manual covering layouts, color palettes, typography, icons, components, responsiveness, and accessibility for MudBlazor-based web applications.
executive_summary: This is the 'Design' chapter (Process 3) of an internal Agile process manual for building consistent web apps in MudBlazor + Blazor. It defines screen templates (login, dashboard, tables, user lists), a primary/secondary color hierarchy with hex values for light/dark modes, WCAG-aligned accessibility contrast rules, a Font Awesome icon catalog mapped to functions (edit, delete, expand), button hierarchy with state behavior, breakpoints, and responsive typography. It is an in-house style guide rather than a tutorial — its job is to make every project the team ships look and behave the same way.
suggested_metaphor: A design system manual is like a kitchen's mise en place: before any chef starts cooking, the salt is in this jar, the knives are at this angle, and the plates are stacked over here. Nobody has to improvise where the pepper lives, so every dish that leaves the pass tastes consistent — even when six different cooks made them.
suggested_intro_hook: Why does one app feel polished and another feel like five different developers fought a war inside it? Almost always because the polished one had a written rule for where buttons go, what red means, and which icon represents 'delete' — and the other one didn't.
what_it_teaches: How to formalize the visual and interaction layer of a Blazor/MudBlazor application: which screens are templates, which colors mean which things, where icons sit, how layouts collapse on mobile, and what minimum contrast and touch targets must be met for accessibility compliance.
key_takeaways: Limit primaries to 1-3 colors; derive hover/active/disabled states by adjusting brightness 20-30%
Feedback colors (success/error/alert/info) must be distinct from brand colors to avoid confusion
Maintain WCAG AA (4.5:1) contrast minimum for text; AAA (7:1) for critical content
Touch targets must be at least 44x44px (preferably 48x48px on mobile) with 8-16px spacing
Use breakpoints XS<600, S<960, M<1280, L<1920, XL<2560 aligned with the 12-column MudBlazor grid
quality_notes: Comprehensive and well-organized as a reference document, but written as a checklist/specification rather than a teaching narrative. Some sections (Tipografia, Animações, Acessibilidade detail, Documentação de exceções) are stub headings without filled-in content — looks like a work-in-progress manual. Icon table is partially garbled by PDF text extraction (column ordering jumbled).

title: Blazor Server For Dummies
one_line_summary: An analogy-driven beginner's guide to 13 essential Blazor Server patterns covering base classes, EF Core configuration, ServiceResult, adapters, bulk operations, security, claims, protected storage, localization, and JS interop.
executive_summary: This is the developer's own 'For Dummies' style explainer of the foundational patterns behind a Blazor Server application — written with everyday analogies (pizza shops, moving trucks, festival wristbands, sticky notes) and minimal code. It walks through three parts: Building Blocks (base entities, EF Core configs, ServiceResult, adapters, bulk ops), Security (roles, BCrypt, sessions, CSRF, claims), and Blazor-specific gotchas (ProtectedLocalStorage, localization, JS interop, prerendering pitfalls). The unifying lesson is that authentication and storage in Blazor are simpler than ASP.NET Identity tutorials make them look — you can build claims yourself.
suggested_metaphor: Learning Blazor patterns from this guide is like getting handed a chef's notebook full of doodles instead of a textbook: every page has a sketch — a pizza shop, a wristband, a moving truck — and somewhere underneath the sketch is the recipe. You learn the ServiceResult pattern not because you memorized 'discriminated union of success and failure', but because you remember that online order tracking emails told you 'Shipped!' or 'Wrong address!'.
suggested_intro_hook: Why does every Blazor tutorial start by importing 47 ASP.NET Identity tables when all you really wanted was to know whether the logged-in user can click the delete button? This guide is the antidote — it tells you the actual mechanism (claims) and lets you build the rest yourself.
what_it_teaches: The minimum viable mental model for building a real Blazor Server app: how to share fields across entity classes, how to configure EF Core cleanly, how services should report success or failure, how to make modules reusable across user types, how to import data fast, how to authenticate users without ceremony, and where browser-only code is allowed to live in the Blazor lifecycle.
key_takeaways: Use base entity classes (BaseEntity with Id, CreatedAt) so adding UpdatedAt later is one edit instead of 20
Put each EF Core entity config in its own file, then call ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly once
ServiceResult<T> with Success/Data/Errors lets services report failure without throwing or returning null
BCrypt is intentionally slow (3 hashes/sec vs MD5's 180 billion) — that slowness is the security
[Authorize] is just checking claims — you don't need ASP.NET Identity to build them yourself
Browser-only code (localStorage, JS interop) MUST live in OnAfterRenderAsync, not OnInitializedAsync, because of Blazor Server's prerender phase
quality_notes: Excellent beginner pedagogy — every concept is bookended with an analogy, code examples are short, and the cheat sheets at the end are useful. Best feature: it explicitly tells the reader 'you don't need ASP.NET Identity', which is a rare and valuable contrarian take. Could go deeper on async/await nuances and SignalR (which underpins Blazor Server) but those are likely covered in other docs.

title: Sistema de Serviço de Stock - Documentação Técnica (PT)
one_line_summary: Portuguese formal technical documentation of the BioBraga stock service: a high-performance inventory tracking system with multi-layer caching, SQL function integration, decorator pattern, and task pre-loading.
executive_summary: This is the formal Portuguese-language technical document for the production stock service in the BioBraga project. It defines the IStockService interface, the StockService base implementation, and the CachedStockService decorator that wraps it with IMemoryCache. The system uses SQL Server table-valued functions (fn_ArtigoStockByDate, fn_ArtigoUsedInFluxo) for heavy aggregation, IDbContextFactory for connection pooling, and a graduated cache expiration strategy (1 hour for historical data >7 days, 5 minutes for recent data). The Razor UI (ArtigoDetalhe.razor) preloads stock as fire-and-forget tasks during OnInitializedAsync so the user perceives instant response when clicking the stock tab.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: The BioBraga inventory module needs to answer 'how many of this article are in stock right now (or on this past date)?' instantly, even though the underlying calculation is a complex aggregation across CrmDocumentoDetalhes, CrmDocumentos, and CrmTipoDocumentos tables that costs ~2 seconds when run cold. Without intelligent caching the article-detail page would be unusable. The system also needs to distinguish historical data (immutable, can be cached for an hour) from today's data (still moving, cache only 5 minutes).
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Provides real-time and historical stock queries via IStockService with four core operations: GetArticleStockByDateAsync (point-in-time stock balance), GetStockMovementsAsync (filtered movement history), GetStockTotalsAsync (aggregated entradas/saidas), and CheckFluxoAsync (per-line document flow check). A CachedStockService decorator wraps the base implementation with IMemoryCache, generating cache keys like 'stock_{artigoId}_{yyyyMMdd}' and applying graduated expiration. Performance metrics reported: cached queries run in 1-2ms versus 1500-3000ms cold.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: StockService calls the SQL function fn_ArtigoStockByDate directly via raw ADO.NET (DbCommand + SqlParameter) because EF Core's overhead is unnecessary for a single-row lookup; it adds a day to the input date to get end-of-day inclusion. GetStockMovementsAsync uses LINQ joins across four tables filtered by Movstocks=true and date range. The CachedStockService checks IMemoryCache, falls through to the inner service on miss, and chooses 1-hour vs 5-minute expiration based on whether the date is older than 7 days. The Razor page initializes a Task<ArtigoStock> field as fire-and-forget during OnInitializedAsync so when the user clicks the stock tab, the awaited task is usually already complete. DI registration uses a manual factory to wire the decorator around the inner service.

suggested_metaphor: The stock service is like a librarian with a photographic memory and a stack of bookmarks: when you ask for a book she's already fetched recently, she hands it to you instantly from her desk; for older books she has the catalog number memorized but still has to walk to the shelves. And while you're still browsing the introduction, she's already gone to fetch the books she predicts you'll ask for next — that's the preload pattern.
suggested_intro_hook: Imagine a warehouse worker asking 'how many of this part did we have last Tuesday?' and the system taking three seconds to answer. Now imagine three workers asking it simultaneously. Now imagine a hundred. This document is how that question went from 3000ms to 1ms.
what_it_teaches: How to build a production-grade caching layer using the decorator pattern in .NET, why graduated expiration beats fixed TTLs, when to drop EF Core for raw ADO.NET, and how to use fire-and-forget Task fields in Blazor to mask latency behind UI navigation.
key_takeaways: Wrap real services with decorators rather than putting cache logic inside them — keeps SRP intact
Use graduated expiration: immutable historical data can cache for hours, recent data only minutes
Skip EF Core for tight single-row lookups; raw DbCommand calling SQL functions is much faster
Preload expensive operations as Task<T> fields in OnInitializedAsync — by the time the user clicks the tab, the result is ready
Don't cache filtered or per-transaction queries — they're too specific to ever be hit again
Always measure: this doc shows 99.9% latency reduction (2000ms -> 1ms) for cached queries
quality_notes: Excellent applied-implementation document — has all four pillars (architecture diagram, interface definition, implementation code, performance metrics, configuration, troubleshooting). The Mermaid sequence diagram is preserved as text. PT version of the same English Stock Service doc; treat as a sibling for the same domain.

title: Named Tuples - Value Semantics, Zero-Allocation, Destructuring
one_line_summary: C# named tuples solve the 'anonymous types can't leave the method' problem with a writable type that has value semantics, stack allocation, and free destructuring.
executive_summary: This is tutorial #32 in a numbered C# language series. It explains why anonymous types are useless for return values (they have no nameable type), introduces named tuples as the C# 7 solution, and walks through a real LINQ example (FindTopCustomers) where the return type is List<(int CustomerId, decimal TotalSpent)>. The tutorial then covers four crucial properties: value semantics (copies are independent, no shared mutation), zero-allocation (lives on the stack, no GC pressure in hot loops), free destructuring (var (id, total) = customer), and a 'when to use what' decision matrix (anonymous type -> tuple -> record -> class as needs grow).
suggested_metaphor: Anonymous types are Post-it notes — perfect for scribbling something at your desk, but you cannot mail them. Named tuples are envelopes — you can write on them, seal them, and send them across method boundaries to anyone you like. Records are full parcels with labels and tracking numbers, and classes are shipping containers with their own forklift drivers.
suggested_intro_hook: If you have ever started writing a LINQ query, gotten to the second .Select(), realized you needed two values per item, and then sighed and created a throwaway DTO class just so the return type would have a name — this tutorial is the line where that stops happening.
what_it_teaches: How to use named tuples to return multi-field results from methods without creating throwaway DTO classes, what value semantics means in practice (mutation doesn't leak), when stack allocation buys you real performance, how to destructure tuples and your own classes via Deconstruct, and when to graduate from a tuple to a record.
key_takeaways: Syntax swap: new { X = ..., Y = ... } becomes (X: ..., Y: ...)
Tuples have value semantics — assigning to b = a copies the data, mutation doesn't leak
Tuples are stack-allocated ValueTuple structs — zero GC pressure in hot loops that don't persist results
Destructuring (var (id, total) = customer) works on tuples for free; classes can opt in via Deconstruct
Sweet spot is 2-3 fields, pure data, crossing a method boundary; more than that, graduate to a record
Names are compile-time metadata — at runtime it's just ValueTuple<T1, T2> with Item1 / Item2
quality_notes: Very clear pedagogical structure with progressive depth: problem -> solution -> real example -> theory -> performance -> when not to use. The tug-of-war between 'tuples are zero-allocation' and the honest correction 'they live on the heap when stored in a list' is intellectually rigorous. Part of a numbered Education series (#32).

title: Training Flow: From BetterGame to Neuron
one_line_summary: An interactive visualization comparing stochastic versus batch training in a neural network, walking through three call levels (BetterGame -> NeuralNetwork -> Neuron) and showing how gradient accumulation eliminates zigzagging.
executive_summary: This is an interactive HTML educational visualization (likely a Blazor or static HTML page) that breaks neural network training into three responsibility levels: BetterGame (the CEO that decides when to stop), NeuralNetwork.Train (the manager that coordinates a forward + backward pass for one example), and Neuron.Train (the worker that adjusts its own weights). It then contrasts stochastic training (update after every example, causing zigzag) with batch training (accumulate gradients across all examples, then apply one averaged update). Includes step-by-step animations, a side-by-side weight evolution comparison, and a method-by-method drilldown into Train, AccumulateGradients, and ApplyGradients with example arithmetic.
prerequisites: C# basics for the code samples
suggested_metaphor: Stochastic training is like a committee where every member shouts their preferred decision and the chair immediately writes it on the whiteboard before the next person speaks — the whiteboard zigzags through every opinion. Batch training is the same committee, but the chair listens to everyone first, averages the votes on a notepad, and writes the consensus on the whiteboard once. The whiteboard ends up in roughly the same place but the path was much smoother.
suggested_intro_hook: Watch your loss curve during training. If it looks like a heart monitor — jagged spikes everywhere — that's not noise, that's your animals fighting each other. Each new training example is undoing what the previous one taught. Here's how batch training fixes that.
what_it_teaches: How a layered training loop assigns responsibilities (CEO/Manager/Worker analogy), why naive stochastic updates cause zigzagging, how gradient accumulation produces a single balanced update per batch, and what the actual code differences are between Train(), AccumulateGradients(), and ApplyGradients().
key_takeaways: Each level only talks to the level directly below it — BetterGame never touches a Neuron, Neurons don't know BetterGame exists
Stochastic = update after every example (fast but zigzags)
Batch = accumulate all gradients first, divide by count, then apply one averaged update
AccumulateGradients does NOT include the learning rate — that's saved for ApplyGradients so you can tune step size separately
The fix for zigzagging loss curves is almost always batching
Reset accumulators (gradients, count) after every ApplyGradients call
quality_notes: Excellent visual/interactive teaching content; the three-level CEO/Manager/Worker hierarchy is a clean mental model. Heavy use of step-by-step interactive controls (Reset, Next Step, Step Into) suggests this is meant to be opened in a browser as an actual visualization. Text extraction loses interactivity but preserves the structure and code samples. Pairs naturally with the Backpropagation.md doc.

title: Notification Recipient Resolver Pipeline
one_line_summary: An OCP-compliant strategy pipeline that resolves notification recipients by chaining ordered resolvers (Manager, HRAdmin, future ones) without modifying existing code.
executive_summary: This document describes a production strategy-pipeline implementation in an HR system for deciding who gets notified when an employee event occurs. Rather than hardcoding 'send to manager AND HR admins', the system defines an INotificationRecipientResolver interface with an Order property and a GetRecipientUserIdsAsync method, registers multiple resolvers via DI, and orchestrates them through NotificationRecipientService which executes them in order, deduplicates via HashSet, and excludes the action initiator. Two concrete resolvers exist (ManagerRecipientResolver order 10, HRAdminRecipientResolver order 20). Adding a TeamLead resolver requires zero changes to existing code — just a new class and one DI registration.

tutorial_structure.why_it_exists: The HR system needs to send notifications when events occur (attendance check-in, leave request, schedule change). The naive approach would be a switch statement inside each notification call site listing every recipient type, which violates Open/Closed — every new stakeholder type (team leads, department heads, project managers) requires editing the same method. This grows into a god-method that nobody dares touch.
tutorial_structure.what_it_does: Provides a single GetRecipientsAsync(context) call that returns a deduplicated, ordered list of user IDs to notify. The context carries the triggering EmployeeId, the company database, and an optional ExcludeUserId (typically the user who initiated the action so they don't notify themselves). The pipeline supports manager resolution, HR admin resolution, and is extensible to team leads, department heads, etc., simply by writing a new class.
tutorial_structure.how_it_works: INotificationRecipientResolver defines Order and GetRecipientUserIdsAsync. NotificationRecipientService injects IEnumerable<INotificationRecipientResolver> from the DI container, sorts them by Order, calls each one with the context, collects results into a HashSet<int> (which automatically deduplicates), and filters out ExcludeUserId. ManagerRecipientResolver (order 10) navigates UserEmployeeLinkage -> CrmUtilizador.ReportToUser to find the direct supervisor. HRAdminRecipientResolver (order 20) calls INotificationService.GetAdminUserIdsAsync to fetch users with RoleLevel >= 50. New resolvers register via builder.Services.AddTransient<INotificationRecipientResolver, MyResolver>() with no other code changes.

suggested_metaphor: The recipient pipeline is like a relay race where each runner has a number on their back saying when they run, but they all carry the same baton — the context. Runner 10 is the manager, runner 20 is HR, runner 25 is the department head. You can drop a new runner in at position 15 without re-organizing the rest of the team, and the baton (the recipient set) automatically dedupes so nobody gets two notifications even if two runners both think they should notify the same person.
suggested_intro_hook: Picture the kind of switch statement that grows by one case every quarter for two years. Every time a new manager type is added, you have to find that file, find the method, add a case, hope you didn't break the manager logic, redeploy. Now imagine never having to edit that file again. That's what an OCP-compliant pipeline buys you.
what_it_teaches: How to use IEnumerable<TInterface> dependency injection plus an Order property to build a strategy pipeline that respects the Open/Closed Principle, how HashSet<T> handles deduplication for free, how to pass exclusion context through a record, and the file-organization convention for keeping resolver implementations together.
key_takeaways: Inject IEnumerable<TInterface> in ASP.NET DI to receive ALL registered implementations of an interface
Use an Order property on each strategy so callers can control execution sequence without coupling
HashSet<int> for recipient IDs is the simplest deduplication primitive
Pass an ExcludeUserId in the context so action initiators don't notify themselves
Adding a new recipient type should be a one-class, one-DI-line change — anything more violates OCP
Use record types for context DTOs to get value-equality and immutability for free
quality_notes: Clean, well-structured applied doc. ASCII architecture diagram, complete code samples, file location map, related-docs cross-references, even a 'how to add a new resolver' worked example. Could be even better with a sequence diagram of the orchestrator's HashSet flow, but the existing tabular order convention is sufficient. Numbered '15-' so it's part of an Education numbered series.

title: Backpropagation Visual Guide
one_line_summary: Backpropagation is the answer to the credit-assignment problem: hidden neurons get blamed in proportion to how strongly they connect to output neurons that made errors.
executive_summary: This is a short visual guide explaining backpropagation in a simple feed-forward network (6 inputs -> 6 hidden neurons -> 8 outputs). It states the credit-assignment problem (we know output errors but not hidden errors), shows the forward pass with ASCII diagrams, then walks through the backward pass where errors flow through the same weights that carried the forward signal. The key insight is symmetry: a strong weight that helped a signal reach the output also carries proportional blame backward. Includes the hidden-error formula (sum of outputError × weight) and a concise C# code snippet implementing the full backprop loop.
key_concepts: weight as both signal carrier and blame carrier
prerequisites: basic neural network anatomy (inputs, hidden, output, weights)
suggested_metaphor: Backpropagation is like figuring out who's at fault for a missed pass in a soccer team. You know the striker missed the goal — that's the output error. But who's actually responsible? The midfielder who passed the ball at exactly the right angle deserves more blame than the defender who barely touched it. The blame travels backward along the same passes that carried the ball forward, scaled by how involved each player was. That's all backpropagation is doing with weights.
suggested_intro_hook: You can train an output neuron easily — you know what it should have said and what it actually said. But what about the hidden neurons? Nobody wrote down what THEY were supposed to output. The trick is so simple it's almost embarrassing: the same weights that delivered the signal forward will deliver the blame backward.
what_it_teaches: Why training a multi-layer network is non-obvious (the credit-assignment problem), how the backward pass mirrors the forward pass through the same weights, the exact formula and C# loop for computing hidden errors, and the symmetry between weights amplifying signals forward and distributing blame backward.
key_takeaways: Output errors are easy: expected minus actual
Hidden errors are 'sum of (outputError * weight) for every output neuron the hidden neuron connects to'
Strong weights carry MORE blame back, not less — blame is proportional to connection strength
Once you have the hidden error, you train the hidden neurons exactly the same way you train output neurons (using the original inputs)
The same weights that carried signals forward carry blame backward — that's why it's called backpropagation
quality_notes: Concise, well-illustrated with ASCII diagrams, includes both formula and code. Short (520 words) but dense — every paragraph adds something. Pairs naturally with training-flow-visualization.html as a companion. Could expand into multi-layer (more than one hidden layer) backprop but the current scope is appropriate for a fundamentals doc.
